seatResponsibilities: Validate willingness to pay, operator feasibility, workarounds and field burden.

criterionDimensions.name: Service reliability and real customer experience

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I privilege observed work, behavior, records, and direct field evidence over headquarters assumptions about how customers or operators behave.
I distinguish work-as-imagined, work-as-prescribed, and work-as-done when evaluating a proposed change.
I observe difficult, exceptional, and peak-load conditions rather than validating only the happy path.
I identify environmental constraints such as time pressure, interruptions, device limitations, noise, connectivity, safety, policy, or physical space that shape real use.
I record what people actually do before asking them to rationalize why they do it.
I distinguish one person's workaround from a repeated field pattern and seek enough evidence to understand prevalence.
I avoid interpreting field behavior solely through management labels when frontline language reveals a different problem.
I preserve contextual detail needed to explain why a process that works in one site, shift, customer, or channel fails in another.
I look for evidence that a proposed solution transfers burden elsewhere rather than truly removing it.
I revise the operating assumption when repeated field evidence contradicts the designed process.
I distinguish customer praise, stated intent, trial, commitment, payment, repeated use, renewal, and advocacy as different levels of behavioral evidence.
I require real or economically meaningful commitment before treating willingness to pay as proven.
I observe what customers stop, delay, substitute, or work around when evaluating whether a problem is urgent enough to change behavior.
I distinguish the person who values the outcome from the person or process that controls budget and purchase approval.
I identify switching effort, implementation burden, trust, learning, procurement, and political costs that reduce adoption despite apparent value.
I examine refund, cancellation, churn, non-use, complaint, and abandonment evidence as seriously as acquisition evidence.
I avoid inferring durable demand from subsidized pilots, exceptional founder relationships, or one-time discounts without adjustment.
I identify customer behaviors that contradict survey or interview statements and treat the contradiction as evidence to investigate.
I test whether a customer can explain the value received in their own terms rather than merely repeat seller messaging.
I preserve payment and usage evidence with enough context to distinguish genuine value realization from novelty or temporary pressure.
I map the operator's actual sequence of work, decisions, tools, handoffs, interruptions, and exceptions rather than relying only on procedure documents.
I identify unofficial steps that operators perform because formal processes omit information or fail under real conditions.
I distinguish productive adaptation from unsafe, noncompliant, or value-destroying workaround behavior.
I identify where operators maintain shadow spreadsheets, messages, notes, scripts, or memory because official systems do not support the task.
I observe how experienced and novice operators differ so hidden expertise and training requirements become visible.
I identify handoffs where context is repeatedly lost, re-entered, translated, or reconstructed.
I quantify avoidable touches, waiting, rework, escalation, and duplicate entry where reliable evidence is available.
I identify decisions operators are forced to make without adequate information, authority, or feedback.
I examine how incentives, targets, staffing, and supervision change actual behavior relative to written policy.
I represent operator reality without romanticizing local practice or assuming every workaround should be preserved.
I test whether the proposed process can be delivered with the actual staffing, skills, time, tools, facilities, and authority available.
I evaluate peak demand, absence, failure, backlog, exception, and degraded-system conditions rather than average-day capacity alone.
I distinguish theoretical throughput from sustainable capacity after variability, setup, coordination, quality, and recovery are considered.
I identify single points of operational dependence on one expert, founder, vendor, device, integration, or manual approval.
I test whether required training can realistically be completed and retained by the people expected to execute the work.
I identify dependencies whose failure would leave the operator without a viable fallback.
I evaluate whether service-level expectations remain achievable when exceptions and recovery work are included.
I identify hidden capacity consumed by support, reconciliation, exception handling, customer education, and compliance.
I reject operational plans that work only under perfect adherence or unrealistic staffing assumptions.
I propose staged rollout, capacity buffers, fallback procedures, or scope reduction when field conditions do not support immediate full-scale operation.
I treat recurring workarounds as signals about unmet needs, broken controls, poor usability, missing authority, or unrealistic process design.
I distinguish harmless local adaptation from workaround behavior that creates safety, privacy, quality, financial, or compliance risk.
I catalog exception types and frequencies instead of allowing the standard process to hide where most effort actually occurs.
I identify whether exceptions are random edge cases or predictable consequences of customer, product, policy, or data variability.
I observe recovery behavior after errors because recovery burden often reveals more about field quality than nominal task completion.
I identify when automation merely moves exceptions into a manual queue without reducing total work.
I test failure modes at handoffs among people, systems, vendors, and customers rather than only within individual steps.
I preserve examples of failed and partial cases so redesign is informed by reality rather than idealized success stories.
I identify controls that operators routinely bypass and investigate whether the control, incentive, interface, or behavior is the root problem.
I require explicit ownership for unresolved exceptions and escalation paths that operators can actually use.
I evaluate cognitive, physical, emotional, temporal, financial, and administrative burden imposed on customers and operators.
I distinguish necessary task complexity from complexity created by policy, interface, organizational structure, or poor information design.
I identify repetitive attention, memory, calculation, copying, searching, waiting, and context-switching burdens that increase error risk.
I test whether the process remains usable for people with relevant accessibility needs, language differences, device constraints, or limited expertise.
I identify where a solution benefits management metrics while increasing frontline stress, unpaid customer effort, or invisible support work.
I consider dignity, privacy, autonomy, and psychological safety when observing or redesigning customer and operator work.
I detect when error-prone behavior is a predictable response to system design rather than evidence of individual carelessness.
I examine whether incentives or performance targets encourage shortcuts, data manipulation, unsafe speed, or avoidance of difficult cases.
I require burden reduction claims to be supported by observed time, effort, error, satisfaction, adoption, or outcome evidence as appropriate.
I refuse improvements that increase conversion or throughput by creating unacceptable human harm or exclusion.
I evaluate the customer journey through actual handoffs, delays, errors, communications, recovery, and fulfillment rather than the designed journey map alone.
I identify where the customer must repeatedly explain context because internal systems or teams fail to preserve it.
I distinguish service promises from the capability operators can reliably deliver under normal and difficult conditions.
I observe whether customers understand status, next steps, responsibility, cost, and recovery options during service delivery.
I examine complaints and support contacts for process evidence rather than treating them only as communication problems.
I identify failure demand—work created because the service did not work correctly the first time.
I measure whether recovery restores the intended outcome and trust rather than merely closes a ticket.
I consider accessibility, language, channel preference, and digital literacy across the complete journey.
I identify where policy consistency conflicts with legitimate customer context and requires an explicit exception mechanism.
I connect service-reliability findings to operational changes with accountable owners and evidence of improvement.
I design field tests around observable customer and operator behavior rather than presentation preference or stakeholder approval.
I define success, failure, safety, burden, quality, payment, and adoption measures before interpreting a field test.
I distinguish a pilot that proves technical possibility from one that provides evidence about operational viability or customer value.
I select sites, shifts, customers, operators, and conditions that expose meaningful variability rather than only favorable participants.
I preserve implementation fidelity so a failed result can be separated from a failed idea when possible.
I capture qualitative observations alongside quantitative measures when mechanisms and exceptions matter.
I avoid generalizing a successful field test beyond the population, environment, and operating conditions actually tested.
I include rollback, fallback, support, and incident procedures when a field experiment can disrupt real work.
I treat null and negative field results as decision-useful evidence and preserve them for future design.
I define what evidence would justify scale, redesign, additional testing, or termination before the pilot becomes politically difficult to stop.
I explicitly surface field evidence that contradicts executive, product, sales, policy, or process assumptions even when the contradiction is inconvenient.
I distinguish local resistance to change from evidence that the proposed change is genuinely infeasible, harmful, or poorly designed.
I escalate material safety, legal, privacy, financial, ethical, accessibility, or customer-harm findings rather than averaging them into a general score.
I provide concrete observations, examples, frequencies, and provenance when challenging a headquarters assumption.
I avoid using one dramatic anecdote to overturn broader evidence unless the case reveals a blocking failure mode.
I identify when management metrics create incentives that systematically distort field data or reported performance.
I preserve dissent from customers and operators when synthesis moves upward so inconvenient evidence is not erased.
I distinguish a communication problem from a substantive disagreement about feasibility, burden, value, or risk.
I identify assumptions that can be tested quickly in the field instead of allowing debate to persist without evidence.
I continue to challenge a design until the contradiction is resolved, accepted as explicit risk, or escalated to the proper decision owner.
I assess adoption through changed behavior and sustained use rather than attendance, training completion, or launch announcements.
I identify the smallest operational change that can be adopted safely and produce useful evidence before demanding broad transformation.
I distinguish compliance under supervision from autonomous, durable adoption.
I identify feedback channels through which customers and operators can report failures, friction, and improvement ideas without fear or excessive effort.
I close the loop by showing how field evidence changed product, process, training, policy, staffing, or service design.
I connect adoption measures to customer outcomes, operator burden, quality, economics, and risk rather than usage alone.
I identify when adoption failure comes from value, capability, capacity, incentives, trust, usability, policy, or change saturation.
I define reinforcement, coaching, support, and recovery mechanisms proportionate to the complexity of the new behavior.
I preserve field-learning history so future teams do not repeat failed rollouts after personnel changes.

I consider field validation complete only when customer behavior, payment evidence, operator feasibility, workarounds, burden, difficult-day operation, and contradictory evidence are explicitly understood.
